speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Specifically, I will address Members' questions raised in relation to SLA's management of Black and Whites.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And I will refer to the various Parliamentary Questions (PQs) which I will address in the course of this speech.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Why do we continue to maintain such a portfolio of older, historical properties and what is SLA's management strategy for such properties?

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Specifically, what is the process by which residential Black and Whites are leased out?

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And finally, whether, in the case of 26 and 31 Ridout Road, SLA took any unusual steps or measures that deviated from its usual process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It sought at all times to achieve a commercially viable outcome, which would secure its interests, as landlord, and also as manager of state properties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In addition, Minister Shanmugam recused himself, as Minister for Law, from any decisions and discussions related to the issue of his own tenancy, should any matter arise.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is validated by the findings of the independent review conducted by Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security, Mr Teo Chee Hean, which Members heard earlier, as well as the investigation by the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau (CPIB).

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Members would have heard the Senior Minister's speech in this House.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These conclusions were reached after a rigorous investigation by CPIB, which also inquired into SLA's conduct as the landlord.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Numerous SLA officers, both former and current, as well as SLA's property and managing agents (MAs), were interviewed by CPIB officers, some of them on multiple occasions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: SLA's processes were closely reviewed, including through the requisition of contemporaneous documents ranging from emails, the leasing documents and approval chain, to messages on private messaging applications.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Direct Tenancy rules were applied fairly for both rental transactions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There was no corrupt intent on the part of any person, or any inducement given to any individual involved in the processing of rentals.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: No preferential treatment was given to the Ministers and their spouses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There was no disclosure of privileged information in the process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There was also no evidence to suggest any abuse of position by the Ministers for personal gain.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I will then set out SLA's management strategy concerning these older, heritage properties, including Black and Whites.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Next, I will outline SLA's management approach to these properties, covering the questions of marketing, valuation and leasing, which Members have raised.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It would also be useful, as we deal with these commercial questions, to have regard to the state of the residential rental market at the relevant time, a question which Mr Don Wee had posed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai, Mr Don Wee, Mr Gerald Giam and Ms He Ting Ru have asked about SLA's management of black and white bungalows, including its plans for such Black and Whites and the context in which they are maintained, including the broader development plans.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: SLA is the custodian of state land and property.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: One of its key roles is to optimise land resources for Singapore's economic and social development.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: SLA oversees the management of about 2,600 state properties in total.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These include landed and non-landed residential properties, former schools, former army camps and shophouses, for example.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Within this portfolio of properties are older, heritage bungalows, and these include the Black and Whites.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Some Black and Whites are also gazetted as conservation properties under the Planning Act and, consequently, carry the obligations which are imposed on conservation properties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There are other properties which are accorded "protected" status, whilst they are evaluated for conservation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Nos 26 and 31 Ridout Road were designated on 29 November 1991 as conservation properties and they were subsequently gazetted in 1992, as they are two rare and intact remaining historic bungalows built in the early 1900s, whose outstanding architectural quality represents the culture and lifestyle of a period in Singapore's history.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ms He Ting Ru had asked about parameters and guidelines for the grant of conservation status.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As Singapore's conservation authority, the Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) is mandated to identify for protection and conservation properties in Singapore which are of heritage value.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: URA conserves various categories of pre-war bungalows, amongst which the Black and Whites are one category.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These are characterised by a particular architectural style from the early 1900s and are visibly recognisable by the black timber structural frame with white infill plastered walls.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Hipped tiled roofs with wide overhangs and extensive verandas are also common features.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These bungalows are a part of Singapore's history.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Some are located in areas where the British naval and air bases used to be, for example, Sembawang and Seletar.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Both categories, whether conserved or protected, impose obligations on the property owner, such as respecting the key elements of the bungalows in the use of the bungalow, namely, the roofs, the structural members, facades of the building, doors and windows and significant interior features, including staircases, decorative mouldings, double volume spaces.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In managing the older, heritage properties, SLA aims to optimise their usage.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At the same time, however, SLA also has to be responsible and mindful of maintaining these properties to meet their conservation and protected status.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These bungalows were built around the early 1900s and so are about more than 100 years old today, maintained in their original condition.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They are located in a wide range of neighbourhoods, both in the central as well as in other areas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Some of them are found in dedicated estates for Black and Whites, for example, Malcolm Road.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Others are interspersed with other private residential properties that are non-Black and Whites, for example, in the Ridout Road estate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The development plans for these properties are ultimately guided by a few factors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We must, first, have regard to URA's Master Plan, which takes into account the intrinsic heritage value of the properties, amongst other factors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Specifically, the planning parameters assigned to areas with Black and Whites are important considerations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The planning parameters determine how such land can be used and for what purpose.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, whether it can sustain high intensity development, such as high-rise buildings, commercial developments and so on.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Or alternatively, whether it is zoned for low intensity, landed properties only.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Where possible, we will also consider if these properties can be modified for other uses or integrated as part of new developments, with a view to rejuvenating and revitalising the area.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This allows for modernisation of the estate while preserving the property's core heritage value.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In addition, we also take into account that these properties, which are dated to begin with, will require more maintenance and upkeep, and this will cost more.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, these lands are part of our Reserves.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Singapore's overall portfolio of state assets comprises financial and physical assets.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The state should be able to keep land parcels, as a block, where appropriate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, these are considered decisions that take into account a balance of factors, including, as I said, the URA Master Plan.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Specifically, for a heritage bungalow, there is the building itself.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There is also the land on which the building sits and the areas adjacent to the building.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: How this land is utilised is also considered in the context of the URA Master Plan, which sets out a suite of planning parameters to guide our land use to meet our nation's needs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In addition to preserving land, which is a part of our Reserves, we also manage the land use to cater to Singapore's land needs in areas, such as housing, education and commercial uses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Accordingly, over time, SLA has carefully broadened the usage and deployment of these properties to meet the evolving needs of Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Others have been repurposed for different uses, such as commercial and retail, or, for example, food and beverage (F&B).

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: With these parameters in mind, the Government has sought to repurpose our heritage bungalows for various alternative uses, and I thought it would be illustrative for me to cite some examples in this House for Members to appreciate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At the Gallop Extension to the Singapore Botanic Gardens, the bungalow at 5 Gallop Road has been repurposed as a Forest Discovery Centre.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is a public space and serves as a picturesque backdrop to popular picnic grounds for the public.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I am sure some or more Members have visited the Centre.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This was reported in the media in August 2022.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Rochester Park and Nepal Park were developed by the British in the early 1950s to house officers and their families.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The area was given conservation status in 2010.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On this occasion, SLA also works and partners private sector partners to develop the space and to place-make Rochester Commons.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Such properties are not only being used – "such" meaning heritage properties – for purely commercial purposes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For instance, bungalows have been also converted to kindergartens and also, in some cases, serve as a shelter for women undergoing unsupported pregnancies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, we look at a broad range of uses: F&B, commercial and, in some cases, social as well.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In other cases, larger sites, where possible, bearing in mind the circumstances and the location and the Master Plan, a larger site comprising more properties might well be suitable for a wider scale redevelopment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As I said, one has to bear in mind the specific context in which the estate is found and also the Master Plan.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If the Black and Whites are located amidst or amongst a landed enclave, such as Ridout Road or perhaps Nassim Road, an area that is zoned for landed properties, removing the Black and Whites or redeveloping them and the land around them would not change the area much.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The cleared land can only then be similarly used for low intensity development.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It would not be possible to put the site to other uses, for example, some of those examples and occasions that I cited earlier.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Accordingly, to Mr Gerald Giam and Ms He Ting Ru's questions about the Government's development plans for Black and Whites, these plans are driven by master-planning considerations, taking into account specific circumstances of each set of properties, where they are located, but also bearing in mind the intrinsic heritage value and the possible uses that might be made of not just the building but of the location and the site.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: One also has to be sensitive to the surrounding vicinity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As I mentioned, we cannot intersperse commercial activities amidst low-intensity development spots.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And within that entire framework, SLA seeks to optimise social outcomes and occupancy and, ultimately, to generate revenue where possible.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These plans also seek to strike a balance between the preservation of heritage and the need to re-allocate land for other uses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Another related question raised is: why not break down a large plot of land and sell it in smaller parcels?

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is a considered decision that takes into account various factors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: URA, through the Master Plan, assesses the best uses of the land, in the overall context of land allocation in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The planning considerations I have spent some time outlining are also relevant.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And it is not always tenable to break up land into small parcels, situated side by side, but then each having a different use.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It would not place-make and, in some cases, the uses may conflict with one another.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In addition, the state should be able to keep land parcels as a block, where appropriate, as part of its land bank.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And as I mentioned, this gives URA maximum planning latitude when it comes to future master plans.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai and Mr Leon Perera asked about the maintenance of Black and Whites.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As I explained above, a portfolio of such Black and Whites are kept as residential housing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A key reason for the cost is the nature of the conservation requirements for such properties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They are much older than the average property in Singapore and require a lot more care, by way of renovation and maintenance.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is consistent with other similar conserved buildings in Singapore which have to comply with the relevant guidelines imposed on them as a result of either their conservation or their protected status.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The requirements to maintain a conservation property apply to many aspects of the property and are very specific.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, the guidelines will spell out the restoration requirements for the conserved building and the alteration works that can be considered and the interfacing zone between the conserved building, the new additions, if any, around the area.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Renovation and refurbishment of a conserved residential property put up for rent is, thus, not just to ensure that it is in a tenantable condition, but also to comply with the relevant guidelines which protect the heritage value of the property.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: When renovating a conserved or protected building, there is significant prescription on how the works and renovations are to be done.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Features, such as the beams and roof of the property, must remain unaffected to the extent that they reflect the architectural value of the property, which was the reason it was identified for conservation in the first place.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Besides the renovations required under conservation obligations, the interior and facilities of most Black and Whites also require upgrading.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Many Black and Whites are more than 100 years old, and they are not like modern detached houses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Most Black and Whites lack modern amenities, which we often take for granted, and require significant effort to retrofit.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, some may lack air-conditioning, water heaters or even cooking hobs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Members may have seen pictures of some Black and Whites over the last couple of weeks in the press.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And you will see that the condition of these properties prior to tenancy, especially if they have been vacant for a prolonged period, is fairly obvious from the pictures.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Therefore, quite often, incoming tenants have to undertake capital expenditure to upgrade the unit to raise it to modern standards.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But the conservation requirements that I just outlined often impose constraints on how far a tenant can retrofit the properties in question.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Also, unlike owners of a property, tenants can only enjoy the benefits of retrofitting for the duration of the tenancy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is a standard term in such leases that when the tenancy lapses, the property and everything that is upgraded by the tenant at his cost, will be returned to SLA, if SLA wishes to keep the upgrade.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This clause also appears in the tenancies of both 26 and 31 Ridout Road.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In such cases, there is, therefore, a need to find a tenant who is prepared to invest capital to upgrade the unit to meet modern day amenities, accept that the benefits of these investments can only be enjoyed for the duration of the tenancy and take on the risk of a higher rental price to renew, or not renewing and writing off the cost of the capital expenditure altogether.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This limits the pool of prospective tenants for Black and Whites.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Most tenants would prefer a ready-to-move-in property, which they can furnish and almost immediately occupy and not have to fork out capital expenditure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To address this challenge, SLA has been adjusting the structure of tenancies to provide more flexibility.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This ties in with the larger goal of maximising occupancy while ensuring that the tenants are able to keep up and maintain the properties and, where possible, also enhance and add to the property through the tenants' capital expenditure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These are various measures which SLA is taking, amongst others, to manage the category of bungalows that are within its management portfolio to maximise the opportunities for the state to benefit from these properties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Don Wee had asked about the rental rate of state-owned heritage properties benchmarked against the private residential market.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: GFA represents the available live-in space for the tenant.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As between GFA and land area, the former usually has a larger impact on the marketability of the property.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Other factors, such as condition of the property and location, are also relevant.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The following additional points can also be gleaned.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Rental trends of Black and Whites tend to follow the general rental market trends.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For the relevant period 2017 through to 2019, market conditions were weak and generally on a downward trajectory.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is evident from URA's rental index for landed properties which showed a consistent softening of the rental market from 2015 to 2020.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members can also access the handout through the app on their mobile devices.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Members will see that this is data available from URA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It shows the rental index from 2015 through to first quarter 2023, roughly by a quarter basis.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The demand for leasing generally, and Black and Whites specifically, was much lower at that time in the period 2017 to 2019 compared to today.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The occupancy rates of state properties have generally moved in tandem with market conditions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Rents of private detached homes and Black and Whites typically trended in the same direction from 2012 to 2019, though the former plunged more severely from 2020 to third quarter 2022 and recovered more aggressively from late 2022 to 2023.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This trend also has a direct correlation to the occupancy rates at the Ridout properties.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Since 2020, no tenant has requested a pre-termination.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: When the rents by land area of private detached homes in Good Class Bungalow (GCB) areas are compared against Black and Whites, there is also a significant divergence.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: One reason for this is, of course, the average land area for Black and Whites is usually larger than private detached homes in GCB areas.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Various Members of this House, including Mr Louis Chua, Mr Murali Pillai, Mr Don Wee, Ms Hazel Poa and Mr Leon Perera have asked about aspects of the process by which SLA manages such leases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin also asked about SLA's standard tenancy operating procedures.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Therefore, SLA supports social uses, even whilst it seeks to maximise occupancy of Black and Whites.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Managing Black and Whites, like any portfolio of real estate assets, requires an appreciation of market conditions and its dynamics and being adaptable to the demands of the market.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In respect of its portfolio of Black and Whites, some properties are managed directly by SLA, and others are managed by MAs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: SLA diversifies the management of its portfolio to include private sector MAs as they are professional organisations, experienced in managing properties in the public and private markets.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In addition to their expertise, they have their own networks and portals through which they can market the properties that they are managing.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This allows SLA to access a wider market.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: SLA works closely with its MAs, who are incentivised by the terms of the arrangement to maximise occupancy and drive rentals, as well as to reduce costs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The MAs are given a broad discretion to manage the properties, consulting SLA from time to time as may be necessary, depending on the circumstances of each case.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is not uncommon for SLA to become involved in handling the management of a property under an MA's purview, for example, when there are requests beyond the scope of an MA's mandate, for example, when the scope of works to be done exceeds the usual works that would be done by the MA or where discussions arise on issues that the MA does not usually handle, such as privacy, security and other issues.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is when the MA, which serves as the agent, goes back to the principal – in this case, SLA – for directions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: When marketing a property, the aim is to maximise occupancy, which the MAs are incentivised to do under the terms of their agreement with SLA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As with all forms of marketing and advertising, it is necessary to adapt the strategy to match prevailing market conditions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The general market practice in the real estate industry is that when market conditions are good and demand exceeds supply, almost all vacant properties will be posted on public platforms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the case of state properties, this will be the State Property Information Online portal, referred to in its abbreviation as SPIO.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is because in a buoyant market, with strong interest, take-up will be likely.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: When property market conditions are poor, however, and supply exceeds demand, or if occupancy in certain estates is low, SLA and its MAs would avoid listing all vacant properties online.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Listing all properties would result in them visibly competing for the limited demand.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This runs the risk of driving the price down, depressing outcomes for the landlord.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They are listed for at least 14 days.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This practice was implemented following a review in August 2022, taking into account prevailing market conditions at that time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At the material time, in 2018/2019, there was no requirement to list all the properties on SPIO.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: SLA and its MA had the discretion on whether to list the properties they managed on SPIO.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For completeness and context, let me explain SLA's policy and thinking on whether to list its properties on SPIO, driven by the prevailing market conditions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In 2007, experiencing high demand, SLA required open bidding, which, in turn, necessitated listing all residential properties managed by its MAs to be put on SPIO.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The success rate of residential state properties allocated through open bidding dropped.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: SLA then adjusted its policy to allow direct letting for specified estates, particularly for those with less than 80% occupancy.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: SLA's MAs had the discretion to decide how to market the properties which were under their portfolio to maximise outcomes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I should add that these are operational concerns decided by SLA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The usual methods employed by the MAs to market the properties include: (a) listing available properties on property portals; (b) circulating the relevant information through its network of agents; (c) listing on social media as appropriate; and (d) placing "To Lease" or "To Let" signages on the properties themselves.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Ridout Road estate was managed by two professional MAs at the relevant time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Nos 26 Ridout Road and 31 Ridout Road were managed by the same MA and that was DTZ Facilities and Engineering (S) Limited.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They were managing them up to 31 March 2018.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Subsequently, from 1 April, Colliers International Consultancy and Valuation (Singapore) Pte Ltd took over as the MA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In both these cases, as was the case for the entire Ridout Road estate, the MAs decided how the properties would be marketed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They could also tap into, and they did, their network of private agents, advertise on social media and so on, and allow for there to be this exchange of information between agents, who might, for example, in some cases, choose to co-broke the marketing of a property.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim had asked what steps were taken by SLA to market the two properties to be leased.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As highlighted, both of them were under the same MA and they decided on the best way to market them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For 26 Ridout Road, it was marketed by the MA from the time the previous tenant pre-terminated in December 2013.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The usual methods, as I have outlined above, would have been carried out.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The MA then decided to undertake some minor works to make the property more presentable to prospective tenants.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Thereafter, the property was marketed by the MA again.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The usual methods of marketing would have been deployed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The MA had also broadcast the property to their network of private agents who deal with and transact in such properties.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For 31 Ridout Road, the MA undertook the usual methods of marketing as I have outlined above.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In this case, it chose to list the property on SPIO.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In addition, it also granted a local film company access to film an interactive arts performance at the property.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This was then used opportunistically to also showcase the property.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This process, for both properties, was consistent with the approach taken by SLA in all other properties marketed by MAs, with the MAs exercising discretion on how to market the property.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These valuations are conducted by professional valuers within the MA or SLA respectively.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The valuation team uses established industry principles and methods for valuation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Factors, such as location, use, floor area, physical condition of the property and prevailing market conditions, will be taken into account.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The SLA valuation team operates separately and independently from the team in charge of leasing.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: SLA's valuation team uses the direct comparison method when undertaking valuations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is an accepted industry methodology for rental valuations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The premise is that a potential tenant would be willing to pay similar rent to a comparable property that is available for rental and this gives a good gauge of the market.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Hence, when valuing a Black and White, a comparable property is considered, which takes into account the factors identified earlier – location, floor area, condition and so on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The valuation team also has regard to the prevailing market conditions and other contextual factors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For instance, in a falling market, such as in 2018, the valuer takes into account the trends in the neighbouring comparable properties, making adjustments for outliers where appropriate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The valuation is for the purposes of determining the guide rent for a given property.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They, meaning the SLA valuation team, do not know the identities of the prospective tenants or the actual rents eventually negotiated by the parties.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I turn to the final aspect in managing Black and Whites – the leasing process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai, Mr Murali Pillai and Mr Leon Perera have raised specific questions on SLA's bidding process, including how long the bidding was open for 26 Ridout Road after Minister Shanmugam's bid was received.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In general, there are two modalities for leasing of all residential state properties and that includes Black and Whites: the first is open bidding; the other is direct letting.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In this case, both 26 and 31 Ridout Road were allocated on the basis of direct letting.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: During the notice period, either SLA or the MA, depending on which property is being asked about, whether it is under their portfolio or otherwise, will then organise open houses for the property in question.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is subject to the bid meeting the guide rent and satisfying other due diligence checks on the bidder.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The guide rent is not revealed to bidders or their agents in this process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ms Hazel Poa asked about the reason for this six-month period.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The short answer to this is that, after six months, valuations would be outdated as the market might have shifted and the information is less market relevant.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Therefore, it is no longer listed on SPIO after six months.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Under direct letting, the MA or SLA receives the bid offers directly.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Their offers can be accepted if the bids meet or exceed the prevailing guide rent.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The decision as to whether to allocate specific properties to direct letting or open bidding, within an estate for which direct letting is permitted, is left to the discretion of the relevant MA or the SLA portfolio manager.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In making this decision, the following general trend is considered.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Estates identified for direct letting are generally one of two categories: those with low occupancy rates or which otherwise have been assessed to benefit from direct letting due to their specific circumstances.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: One example will be in an estate where many units have become available at the same time, together, such that there is bidding fatigue from the earlier batches of units that were released.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ms Hazel Poa asked if SLA was aware of the identity behind the bid for the leasing of 26 Ridout Road.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As CPIB has established, the valuer did not even know that Minister Shanmugam and SLA had settled on a rent of $26,500.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: She had assessed the guide rent not knowing the identity of the prospective tenant or the rent he had already agreed to pay.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai asked whether the President's agreement is required when not awarding state properties to the highest bidder.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This issue does not arise in the context of the rental of state properties that I have outlined.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For state land and state properties, the President's agreement is required if such land or properties are to be disposed of below fair market value such that there would be a draw on Past Reserves.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The grant of tenancies of state properties by SLA is not a disposal of state properties.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Next, let me turn to the works on the properties.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai and Mr Leon Perera have asked about the improvement and maintenance works carried out at both properties.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For context, Members will recall that both these properties have been gazetted for conservation and SLA is responsible for the maintenance works based on the conservation and restoration guidelines that I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For the main roof, the original profile, pitch, height and eaves projection have to be retained and restored.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Owners are required to keep the original roof tile material, colour and profile, if it is a unique feature of the building.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Structural strengthening or supports like steel or reinforced concrete roof beams, if required to be added, have to be done in a way which is sensitively designed to minimise visual impact on the traditional timber system to be retained.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Another example is the architectural features on the building facades.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The original fanlights, windows, doors and vents are to be retained and restored.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Internally, owners may be required to keep such original finishes of the internal ceiling, wall and floor that give a distinctive character to the building.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Thus, all works have to be done in a manner which preserves the architectural style and features of the "black and white bungalows" as defined by URA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And all of this has a significant impact on the costs of the repairs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Therefore, SLA's practice is to engage an external consultant to assess the state of the property and determine the works which have to be done, bearing in mind the relevant conservation guidelines.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: While these works are done in periodic cycles, where practical, SLA tries to do them in the lead up to a confirmed tenancy, to avoid disrupting existing tenants and to ensure that the costs of the works done can be recovered from a prospective tenant.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For 26 Ridout Road, SLA engaged a consultant who had experience in dealing with heritage properties to survey the property and identify the necessary works to be done.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I would add that this consultant was engaged before a bid was made for 26 Ridout Road.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The works identified by the external consultant were in the nature of structural items, such as timber beams, rafters and columns and other heritage features.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: A similar building management inspection was also undertaken by an external consultant for 31 Ridout Road and the works to be done were identified and proposed by the consultant.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This included extensive works to the roof, which was assessed to be in a bad state, as well as other heritage features.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For 31 Ridout Road, these works, as recommended by the consultant, cost around $452,000 out of the total of $570,500 spent on 31 Ridout Road.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In addition, SLA also did the usual sprucing up works prior to the commencement of a tenancy.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These are the usual works done shortly before the property is handed over to a new tenant to ensure that the property is habitable.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For 26 Ridout Road, the works included painting, pest control and the removal of mould.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For 31 Ridout Road, the works included general repairs to the staircase, the perimeter of the house, fixing windows, painting, pest control and, in this case, also snake combing.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The works done by SLA were in keeping with SLA's general practices, as I described earlier in my speech.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On the clearance of the additional land for 26 Ridout Road, as I mentioned, the costs were fully recovered from the tenant by amortising it through the rental collected over the period of tenancy.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Turning to the works done by the tenants themselves, Minister Shanmugam offered to and did invest in substantial improvement works to the property.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These included a new air-conditioning system, building a new carpark shelter, constructing a swimming pool, installing garden lights and upgrading the toilets as well as adding trees and other planting.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: All improvement works undertaken by the tenant become the property of the landlord and revert to state ownership when the property is returned to SLA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This, as I mentioned earlier, is an established practice for all tenancies requiring capital expenditure.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These works are in the nature of capital expenditures and they seek to enhance the value of the properties.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: URA approved the retention of the pavilion as it did not affect the façade of the conserved building.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Next, Ms Hazel Poa and Mr Leon Perera have asked about the trees within the two properties that were felled.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Both properties are located within the Tree Conservation Area.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Any tree within a Tree Conservation Area with more than a one-metre girth would require National Parks Board (NParks) approval to be felled.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Prior to the tenancy of 26 Ridout Road, trees of less than one-metre girth were removed by SLA as part of the clearing of the additional land.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: NParks' approval was not required for these trees.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: After the tenancy commenced, the tenant periodically raised concerns about the structural and health conditions of the older trees, including, in one instance, after a neighbour expressed concerns about safety.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There were legitimate concerns that some trees, such as decayed trees and those with poor vigour or structural defects, would pose safety issues.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This, in fact, was the specific issue that Minister Shanmugam was concerned about and which explained why he was not keen to have the additional vegetated land fenced into his tenancy.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The legal obligations arising from any mishaps or failure to maintain the land properly within the tenancy boundary falls on the tenant.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On each occasion, before any decision about the tree – any of the trees felled – was made, an arborist was brought in for a tree inspection.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For the trees that were removed, the reports found evidence of various problems that posed safety concerns, such as wound decay on main trunks and on buttress roots.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For 18 of the 19 trees, there were independent arborist reports.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These reports set out the condition of the trees in detail and found either decayed buttress roots, structural defects, termite infestations, poor structural form and vigour, or severe leaning resulting in high potential for failure.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The reports were the basis upon which approval was then sought and obtained from NParks for every one of these trees.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: NParks also conducted site visits to inspect the trees in person, where necessary.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And it was only thereafter that the trees were removed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The one tree which did not require an arborist report had failed in bad weather.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: NParks' approval was obtained to fell or remove the rest of the tree that had already failed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The MA has also replaced 17 trees in the property over the last five years, and the tenant has also replanted trees in the property in addition to those replaced by the MA at his cost.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: No 31 Ridout Road was also in the Tree Conservation Area.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Likewise, felling of any trees with more than a one-metre girth needs NParks' approval.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Likewise, the trees were felled after NParks gave the approval and this was done prior to the start of the tenancy.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai also asked if the process was fair, transparent and competitive.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It found no evidence of corruption or wrongdoing in either of the two rental transactions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It had examined the direct letting of the properties to Ministers Shanmugam and Vivian Balakrishnan and found that they were applied fairly.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The internal processes and standards as regards marketing, valuation and leasing were adhered to scrupulously by SLA, with no preferential treatment being given to either Minister.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Ministers had access only to publicly available information concerning the leases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I have described in detail how SLA handled the process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In addition, both tenants would be making substantial capital expenditure to renovate and enhance the properties.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: SLA would then be able to retain these enhancements at the end of the tenancy period.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This would add value to any subsequent tenancy for SLA, and also be set off against the works which SLA had to undertake to renovate and refurbish the properties which I had taken Members through.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It should also be borne in mind that both these offers were made at a time when the rental market in Singapore was depressed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The previous tenant of 26 Ridout Road had pre-terminated their lease and no viable offers were received in the intervening period for either property.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The terms of both leases were standard and did not contain any unusual clauses.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They were entirely at arms-length and did not deviate from usual processes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The specific valuer handling the request for valuation did not know the potential tenant.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And Senior Minister Teo has explained how Minister Shanmugam had removed himself from the chain of command and decision-making process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: AGO conducts annual audits for Government Financial Statements and these include receipts collected by SLA on MinLaw's behalf.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These receipts include rental income from state land and buildings.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Government Financial Statements audit does not cover the revenue tendering process of state properties as the audit objective in that case is to ascertain whether the receipts reported are accurate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: However, in addition to the annual audits, AGO also carries out selective audits of Statutory Boards in rotation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In a selective audit, AGO has the discretion to decide what areas they choose to audit using a risk-based approach and also decide on the specific timing and timeframe of such audits.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It has provided me with an opportunity to lay out the facts clearly, fully, relating to these two tenancies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I welcome any further clarifications that Members may have subsequently.
